title: AI Cracks 47-Year-Old Math Problem: Anthropic and OpenAI Claim Same-Day Proof of "Algebraic P≠NP"
summary: Anthropic and OpenAI claim same-day proof solving the 47-year-old algebraic P vs NP problem
detailed: Anthropic and OpenAI independently published preprint papers on GitHub claiming proofs for the algebraic P≠NP problem (VP≠VNP) posed by mathematician Leslie Valiant in 1979.

Anthropic's internal Claude model produced a 70-page paper and roughly 73,000 lines of Lean 4 formal verification code, while OpenAI's result was obtained on November 6 and made public on November 23.
Anthropic's proof concludes that arithmetic circuits computing the permanent of an m×m matrix require quasi-polynomial lower bounds exceeding any fixed polynomial power.
Both papers include formal verification code but have not yet undergone peer review by human mathematicians.
sentences: Two artificial intelligence companies have claimed almost simultaneously that their respective models independently solved a mathematical problem that has stood for nearly half a century.

Anthropic and OpenAI successively published papers on the code-hosting platform GitHub, saying they had proved that "VP is not equal to VNP" over arbitrary fields—the "algebraic version of P≠NP" in algebraic complexity theory.
Both papers come with Lean 4 formal verification code, but neither has yet been peer-reviewed by human mathematicians.
Anthropic's paper was uploaded about six hours earlier than OpenAI's, according to people familiar with the matter.
The former was produced by an internal research version of the Claude model, with both the paper and the Lean code written by AI.
The paper runs 70 pages, lists only Claude in the author field, and comes with roughly 73,000 lines of Lean 4 code.

The latter paper is 30 pages and likewise includes a Lean 4 formal proof, but according to OpenAI's own release records, its result was obtained as early as November 6 and only made public on November 23.

A comparison of the public information from the two papers is as follows:
The problem was posed by mathematician Leslie Valiant in 1979 and is the algebraic-computation counterpart of the famous "P vs NP" problem.
At its core is a comparison of the computational difficulty of two classes of polynomials: the determinant and the permanent.
For an m×m matrix, the determinant can be computed quickly within a polynomial-size arithmetic circuit using classical algorithms such as Gaussian elimination.
The permanent's formula is almost identical to the determinant's, except that all the minus signs are changed to plus signs.

Intuitively, removing the cancellation between positive and negative terms should make it simpler, but the opposite is true—precisely because this "shortcut" is absent, the computational complexity of the permanent explodes.
Valiant conjectured on this basis that no polynomial-size arithmetic circuit can compute the permanent—that is, VP≠VNP.

In computational complexity theory, VP represents the class of functions computable by polynomial-size arithmetic circuits, while VNP corresponds to objects such as the permanent and the Hamiltonian cycle polynomial.
Proving that VP is a proper subset of VNP would mean that problems that are intrinsically hard to compute genuinely exist in the algebraic world.

The conclusion Anthropic reaches in its paper goes further: over any field of characteristic not equal to 2, an arithmetic circuit computing the permanent of an m×m matrix must have more than m to the power of c·(log₂m)^{1/3} gates, where c is a constant greater than zero.
This magnitude overtakes any fixed power of a polynomial as m grows, but remains far below exponential—what academics call a "quasi-polynomial" lower bound.
For the Hamiltonian cycle polynomial, the same lower bound holds over fields of any characteristic.
The best lower bound previously known to academia had stood since 1983 and had never exceeded the order of m²·log m.

Notably, Claude's proof did not attack the permanent directly.

Instead, it transformed the problem into a polynomial related to network connectivity, or into a polynomial for a general automaton with weighted halting branches, and then transformed the tensor rank problem in algebra into a distance problem in a certain geometric space.
The key step in the paper is to prove that this geometric space has non-positive curvature and to split the situation in two: either "flat" or "contracting," with at least one necessarily holding.
Claude explicitly acknowledges in the paper that even over the most basic field of real numbers, it cannot determine which case actually holds in reality.
The two paths ultimately converge on the same conclusion: no small-size arithmetic circuit exists for the permanent.
OpenAI's paper likewise claims to establish VP≠VNP, but the two proofs differ in their technical routes.
It is not yet possible for outsiders to judge which path has greater generalizable value.

Academia responds with caution: formal verification is not mathematical consensus
Formal verification is the translation of a mathematical argument into code that a computer can check line by line.
Both papers used Lean 4 for end-to-end checking, and Anthropic says its more than 300 Lean files and roughly 73,000 lines of code have passed checks by two independent verification kernels.

But formal verification can only guarantee that the reasoning steps are logically sound; it cannot replace human mathematicians' judgment of the proof's approach, conceptual innovation, and generalizability.
More critically, Lean only guarantees that the proposition written in Statement.lean can be derived from Mathlib and three standard axioms.

As for whether these formal definitions faithfully correspond to Valiant's original VP and VNP, no human mathematician has confirmed that either—according to the paper's appendix, even this comparison step was performed by another AI.
Anthropic also states explicitly in the paper that the proof was discovered and written by AI and has not been reviewed by any human mathematician.

According to a report by Notebookcheck, Tom Gur of the University of Cambridge described the development as "unprecedented," saying that decades of mathematical work appeared to have been advanced within days.
But he also stressed that the mathematics community needs more time to study these proofs and judge how far their techniques can be generalized.
Varun Kanade of the University of Oxford believes the results may bring researchers closer to solving P vs NP, but that entirely new techniques will most likely still be needed.

Ben Livshits of Imperial College London noted that such rapid progress has sparked broader discussion about the future direction of theoretical computer science and the role of AI in mathematical research.
The verification process itself is also under pressure.

The algebraic world is breached; the Boolean world remains locked
It should be made clear that this result does not solve the classic P vs NP problem.
Anthropic states explicitly at the end of its paper that the team solved VP vs VNP, not P vs NP, and pinpoints the two specific steps that would fail on Boolean circuits.

Arithmetic circuits require addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division steps to work uniformly for all elements in the field and in extension fields, and cannot perform bit operations tailored to 0 and 1; Boolean circuits are not subject to this constraint.
Therefore, the breakthrough in the algebraic world cannot yet open the door to the Boolean world.

An existing result cited in the paper shows that, over a suitable field, VP=VNP would imply P/poly=NP/poly; but conversely, there is currently no known method for deriving a separation of Boolean circuit classes from VP≠VNP.
In addition, although this proof crosses the "super-polynomial" threshold, it only barely does so.
The best known upper bound for computing the permanent is currently exponential, and a huge gap still lies between the two.
For the AI industry, the significance of this event may lie not in the mathematical conclusion itself but in the shift in the R&D paradigm.
Both companies completed the entire process—from problem discovery and paper writing to formal verification—in an extremely short time, and Anthropic's paper lists only the model in its author field.

This provides a testable sample of AI-assisted scientific research: the value of model output is no longer limited to text generation but can produce formal results that machines can check line by line.

If such capabilities continue to mature, fields that rely on complex computation and formal reasoning—such as pharmaceuticals, materials, and cryptography—may be the first to see their research processes restructured.

At the same time, the scarcity of verification capacity will become a new bottleneck: when AI produces proofs faster than human mathematicians can read them, how to allocate review resources and establish credible machine-verification standards will become a challenge facing academia and industry alike.

In the secondary market, the event is unlikely to translate directly into revenue or profit in the short term, but it reinforces both companies' brand positioning in "frontier reasoning capabilities" and may also boost corporate clients' expectations of demand for AI research tools.
Given that neither paper has been peer-reviewed, any judgment about technology roadmaps based on them should be made with caution.
The Clay Mathematics Institute has moved the Riemann Hypothesis and the Navier-Stokes equations into its "Active problems" category.
At present, the Millennium Prize Problems still listed as "unsolved" are P vs NP, Yang-Mills existence and mass gap, the Hodge conjecture, and the BSD conjecture—four in total.
